services: Matins of the All-Night Vigil: the Polyeleos, with Psalm 134

about.what: A psalm of thanksgiving, the hundred and thirty-fifth as the Church counts the psalms, by the Septuagint. Its twenty-six verses give thanks for the works of God, in creation and in bringing Israel out of Egypt, and every one of them ends with the same answer, “for his mercy endures for ever”, quoted here in Brenton's English.
about.history: Psalm 135 is the second of the two psalms of the Polyeleos, after Psalm 134, which opens “Praise ye the name of the Lord”. Hapgood's Service Book prints them at Matins of the All-Night Vigil, sung with Alleluia when the holy door is opened and the priest censes the sanctuary, the holy images, the people and the whole temple (1906, p. 28, where the two psalms are numbered cxxxv and cxxxvi, as in the Hebrew). Its notes give the sense of the name: from the Greek for much and for mercy, or oil, because these psalms repeat the word mercy, and because the lamps are lit while they are sung (Appendix B, p. 595).
about.when: At Matins of the All-Night Vigil, kept on the eve of Sundays and feasts, after the readings from the Psalter: the Polyeleos (Hapgood, pp. 15 and 28).

lines.unsure: Sung long, with a breath halfway (at 4:06.5): perhaps a second Alliluia. One line holds both until a listener who knows the chant confirms it.

variants.wordsSource: All ten verses the choir sings (1 to 6 and 23 to 26), in its order, each half followed by the Alliluia it sings. The first verse is as the owner took it down beside the recording, in Latin letters, set here in Arabic letters by Purify, and a speech model heard it word for word (i'tarifu lir-Rabbi fa-innahu salihun, Alliluia, fa-inna ila l-abadi rahmatahu, Alliluia), sung without the h of the Arabic Bible's hallelujah; the same refrain and Alliluia close every verse. The choir sings the first half of the other nine verses in the Antiochian Church's own Arabic, and no public-domain printing of that wording has been found, so each of those nine lines is the nearest public-domain wording, printed verbatim from the Van Dyck Arabic Bible (1865; Psalm 136 in its count), and not the words sung. Each line is timed to the recording, word by word. The transliteration is ours.

variants.wordsSource: The words the choir sings, line by line, each line printed verbatim from a public-domain English psalter: the King James Version (1611), which has the choir's “O give thanks unto the Lord” and its refrain “for his mercy endureth for ever”, and where the King James words differ from the singing, the line of the printing nearest to it: Brenton's Septuagint (1851), Thomson's Septuagint (1808), the American Standard Version (1901) or the Douay-Rheims (Challoner). The choir sings a modern psalter whose own wording is not copied; where no public-domain printing has a sung line, the nearest printed line stands, and each line's printing and what is sung beside it are listed in docs/chants/psalm-135-english.md. After each half, the Alleluia the choir sings, the psalm's own first word in Brenton. Each line is timed to the singing.
